chapters.title: Chapter 8: Careers and the Business of Market Making in India

lessons.title: A Realistic First 90 Days on a Market Making Desk

body.text: The first 90 days are not about inventing a new strategy. They are about earning the trust to touch a live, already-working system, one small, closely supervised piece at a time.

children.text: Weeks 1 to 2: Learning the System, Not Building One

A new hire's first two weeks are typically spent reading, not building: the desk's existing codebase, how its own version of the reservation price and spread logic from Chapter 3 is actually implemented, which is usually a far more heavily tuned and instrumented version than any textbook formula, and how its risk limits and kill switch from Chapter 5 are configured. Almost nobody is handed live trading authority in this window. The realistic expectation is shadowing a senior researcher or trader, asking narrow, specific questions, and being assigned small, well-scoped tasks, cleaning a dataset, writing a monitoring dashboard, rather than anything resembling designing a strategy from scratch.

A typical first real contribution is bounded and easily reversible: building a spread capture rate or fill ratio dashboard for one specific instrument, using Chapter 6's metrics, estimating a single parameter like κ or γ for one narrow contract under a senior researcher's direct review, or proposing one small, specific, tested change to a risk parameter that a senior signs off on before it ever touches live capital. Nothing here risks real money without someone more experienced reviewing it first, which is a feature of a well-run desk, not a sign of being under-trusted.
Weeks 7 to 12: First Real Ownership, Still Within Guardrails

By around the second or third month, a new hire who has shown solid judgment on small tasks often gets ownership of a genuinely narrow slice of the book, one illiquid contract, or one specific parameter within a much larger system, still under a senior's oversight. This is usually the first point where a new hire's own analysis or parameter tuning visibly moves small amounts of real P&L, and where they start participating, even if only in an advisory capacity at first, in the escalation decisions from Chapter 3's case study, and start being evaluated on their own narrow scope using the exact metrics from Chapter 6.

cells: Reading the codebase, shadowing, small scoped tasks
Touching live trading parameters or capital
Bounded, reviewed contributions: dashboards, single-parameter estimation
Making unreviewed changes to a live system
Narrow ownership of one contract or parameter, under oversight
Independent authority over the full book or major risk limits

children.text: Four things tend to surprise people who join expecting something closer to how trading is often portrayed. First, how much of the actual daily work is data cleaning and infrastructure rather than glamorous, split-second decisions. Second, how conservative and incremental real risk-taking is, compared to a popular image of trading as constant high-stakes gambling. Third, how much of a typical day is spent monitoring the metrics from Chapter 6 and reacting to what they show, rather than inventing new pricing theory from a blank page. Fourth, how central regulatory awareness from Chapter 5, algo registration, order-to-trade ratios, kill switch readiness, actually is to daily work, rather than being an occasional compliance afterthought.

body.text: None of this should read as discouraging. It is, if anything, good news for anyone who has worked seriously through this course: the actual daily reality of the job rewards exactly the careful, metric-driven, incrementally verified way of thinking this course has modelled throughout, not a dramatic, high-variance style of decision-making.

body.title: A New Hire Wants to Change Something Now
body.scenario: A new hire, two weeks into the job, is confident that one of the desk's existing risk parameters is set too conservatively and wants to convince their manager to loosen it immediately across the whole book.
body.prompt: Using this lesson's framework for how the first 90 days typically work, what would be a more realistic and more persuasive way for this new hire to pursue this idea?
body.modelAnswer: Rather than asking for an immediate, book-wide change, a more realistic approach is to propose a small, bounded, reversible test: applying the change to one narrow contract, under a senior's review, and measuring the effect using Chapter 6's own metrics, spread capture rate, fill ratio, drawdown, before and after. This matches exactly how real contributions get made in weeks 3 to 6 of a typical first 90 days, and it gives the manager concrete, low-risk evidence to evaluate rather than asking them to accept an untested change across the entire book from someone two weeks into the job.

body.title: What Actually Fills a New Hire's Early Days
body.question: According to this lesson, what typically fills the largest share of a new hire's first two weeks on a market making desk?
options: Independently trading live capital from day one
Reading the existing system, shadowing senior staff, and completing small, well-scoped tasks
Designing an entirely new pricing model from scratch
Immediately taking over risk limit decisions for the whole book
body.explanation: The realistic pattern is understanding an already-working system before touching it: reading code, shadowing experienced staff, and handling small, bounded tasks. Live trading authority, new strategy design, and book-wide risk decisions all come later, if at all, and only after smaller, closely reviewed contributions have built up trust.

points: The first two weeks are typically spent reading and shadowing, not building or trading
Early contributions are small and reversible: dashboards, single-parameter estimation, and reviewed proposals rather than unsupervised live changes
Real, if narrow, ownership tends to arrive around the second or third month, still within a senior's oversight

New hires are commonly surprised by how much of the job is data and infrastructure work, how conservative real risk-taking is, how metric-driven daily work actually is, and how central regulatory awareness is to it
The careful, incremental, metric-driven approach this course has modelled throughout maps directly onto how a real first 90 days actually unfolds
This closes Chapter 8's arc on the people and business side of market making; the final chapter brings every tool from this course together into one continuous capstone case study
